analysis.one_liner: Requires websites and online services to notify users and get consent before collecting or selling personal data.
analysis.headline: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill with bipartisan support and put it on the Senate calendar in August 2002, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set the first federal baseline for internet privacy. Websites, internet providers, and online services would have to tell users what personal information they collect and who it goes to, get explicit permission before collecting sensitive data like health, religion, political party, or financial records, give users an opt-out for everything else, warn users when their data is breached, and let users see and correct their own files. The Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and individual users could all enforce the rules. The bill cleared its committee with bipartisan support but was never brought to a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, who would gain control over how companies collect, use, and sell their personal information, including health, religious, political, sexual orientation, and financial data.

how_it_helps.text: Websites and online providers could not collect or share a user's name, address, or phone number without clear, conspicuous notice of what is being collected and who it will be disclosed to.

Collecting sensitive data — health information, race, political party, religious beliefs, sexual orientation, Social Security numbers, or financial records — would require the user's affirmative written or electronic consent beforehand.

For other personal data, companies would have to give robust notice at the point of collection and a genuine opportunity to opt out, and users' choices would follow their data even if the company was bought or went bankrupt.
Companies would have to notify users when their personal data was compromised by a hacker, a failure of the company's own systems, or a violation of the law.
Users could request access to and correction or deletion of information held about them, and companies would have to maintain reasonable security procedures for the data they keep.

Violations would be enforceable by the FTC as unfair or deceptive practices, by state attorneys general on behalf of residents, and by users in court, with damages of actual loss or $5,000 for misuse of sensitive data, up to $100,000 for repeated knowing violations.
Employees who report their company's violations would be protected from being fired, and the rules would apply to federal agencies and to the Senate's own operations.

analysis.who_pays: Internet service providers, commercial websites, advertising networks, and companies that buy and sell consumer data, which would bear compliance costs and lose revenue from collecting and reselling user information.
analysis.who_pays_short: Websites, ad networks, and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state privacy laws, so any state that wanted stronger protections for its residents could not go further than this federal baseline.

Companies could comply through FTC-approved self-regulatory 'safe harbor' programs rather than meeting the statutory rules directly, which critics could see as reintroducing the industry self-policing the bill's own findings called insufficient.

Businesses with under $1 million in annual revenue and fewer than 25 employees are exempt entirely, and the private right of action covers only sensitive data, requires a showing of actual harm to recover damages, and is capped.
Companies may charge users up to $3 to see their own records, though unemployed people, welfare recipients, and fraud victims get free access.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and the enforcement tools are stronger than typical for privacy bills, including a private right of action and state attorney general suits. The trade-offs are meaningful but not fatal: preemption of state law locks in one national baseline, the self-regulatory safe harbor and small-business exemption give companies easier outs, and recovery in court is limited to sensitive data with actual harm. On balance the bill would have given internet users substantially more control over their data than the largely unenforceable self-regulation then in place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the Senate Commerce Committee favorably and was placed on the Senate's calendar on August 1, 2002, but the Senate never called it up for a vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Fritz Hollings introduced the bill on April 18, 2002 with ten cosponsors, including two Republicans, Senator Ted Stevens and Senator Conrad Burns.

The Senate Commerce Committee held hearings on April 25, 2002, ordered the bill reported favorably on May 17, and formally reported it on August 1, 2002 with an amendment in the nature of a substitute and written minority views.

The committee-passed version required opt-in consent for sensitive data, opt-out for other data, breach notification, user access and correction rights, and enforcement by the FTC, state attorneys general, and individual users.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on August 1, 2002, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from collecting, profiling, and selling internet users' personal information are better off, since no federal privacy baseline was enacted. Companies that wanted a single national standard were also spared a patchwork of state rules, though the state rules never materialized either.

for.name: Sen. Fritz Hollings
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, chaired its hearings, and reported it favorably out of committee with an amended substitute version.

against.name: Internet and advertising industry
against.role: Companies and trade groups that profit from collecting and reselling user data
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against comprehensive federal online privacy legislation, urging that privacy be handled through industry self-regulation instead.

against.name: Senate floor leadership
against.role: Controls which bills come to the Senate floor for a vote
against.what_they_did: Never called the bill up for a vote after it was placed on the Senate calendar in August 2002.

against.name: Senate Commerce Committee minority
against.what_they_did: Filed minority views with the committee report on August 1, 2002, registering their disagreement with the bill as reported.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship and committee support were bipartisan — ten cosponsors including two Republicans, and a favorable committee report — but the committee report carried written minority views, and the bill's opponents online were mostly industry and self-regulation advocates rather than a party bloc.

industries.note: The bill covers third parties including advertising networks and firms that distribute tracking software, and bans selling or sharing user data without notice and consent. These companies' revenue depends on the collection and resale of personal information that the bill would have restricted.

industries.industry: Internet service providers and commercial websites
industries.note: They would bear compliance costs, appoint privacy officers, and lose the ability to monetize user data without consent. But the bill's preemption of state law would have spared them a patchwork of stricter state rules, and FTC-approved self-regulatory programs and the small-business exemption offered ways to lighten the burden.
Businesses with under $1 million in revenue and fewer than 25 employees are exempt from the bill's requirements entirely.
